content.overview: Water-quality control is only as reliable as the measurements. pH and EC instruments can drift, foul or respond incorrectly if probes are stored, cleaned or calibrated improperly. Measurement quality needs its own routine and records.

vocabulary.definition: Adjustment of an instrument using standards with known values.
A check that confirms an instrument performs acceptably without necessarily changing its calibration.
Change in instrument response over time that creates systematic measurement error.

sections.title: Calibrate with appropriate standards
sections.body: Use fresh, appropriate standards and follow manufacturer storage/temperature instructions rather than assuming a meter remains accurate indefinitely.

sections.title: Verify before diagnosing the crop
sections.body: When a reading changes unexpectedly, compare against a reference solution or second verified instrument before redesigning irrigation or nutrition around one sensor.

sections.title: Records reveal recurring instrument issues
sections.body: Log calibration date, standards, slope/error where available, cleaning, probe replacement and verification failures so measurement quality is auditable.

workedExamples: A sudden pH shift that appears only on one aging probe should be verified before changing the whole reservoir.
An EC meter coated with fertilizer residue can produce a systematic error that looks like a crop-management problem.
commonMistakes: Calibrating only after impossible readings appear.
Changing crop inputs before verifying the measuring tool.
content.practicalApplication: Create a meter-control log with device ID, calibration/verification frequency, standard lot/date, cleaning and out-of-tolerance response.
content.summary: Reliable irrigation decisions require controlled measurement tools, not merely digital displays.
